resources.title: Further Maths formulae sheet
resources.summary: The formulae on AQA's Further Maths formulae sheet, grouped as the sheet groups them, plus the cylinder formulae it leaves off and the ones printed in a question when it needs them.
resources.statusNote: Follows AQA's sheet, which is marked "for exams in June 2027 only". No sheet is confirmed for 2028. Ofqual's decision to keep formulae sheets from 2028 names GCSEs, and Further Maths is a Level 2 Certificate, not a GCSE. AQA's specification says students "are expected to know" most of these formulae and that they "will not be given in the exam". So learn them, and use the sheet if you are given one.

items.name: Identities
items.symbols: For any angle $\theta$. Example: if $\sin\theta = \tfrac{3}{5}$ and $\theta$ is acute, $\cos^2\theta = 1 - \tfrac{9}{25} = \tfrac{16}{25}$, so $\cos\theta = \tfrac{4}{5}$ and $\tan\theta = \tfrac{3}{4}$

items.name: A straight line
items.symbols: Through $(x_1, y_1)$ with gradient $m$. Through $(2, 5)$ with gradient $3$: $y - 5 = 3(x - 2)$, which is $y = 3x - 1$

items.name: A circle
items.symbols: Centre $(a, b)$, radius $r$. Centre $(3, -2)$ and radius $5$: $(x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25$. The point $(6, 2)$ is on it, since $3^2 + 4^2 = 25$

applications.title: Satellite navigation
applications.body: A phone finds your position by working out distances from satellites and solving where circles, and in three dimensions spheres, of those radii meet: the circle equation, scaled up.

applications.title: Engineering drawings
applications.body: A designer placing a curved joint needs the tangent to a circle at a point. The tangent is at right angles to the radius, so its gradient is $-1$ divided by the gradient of the radius, and the straight line equation does the rest.

resources.title: Must-know results
resources.summary: The results Further Maths uses that no sheet prints: differentiation, tangents and normals, stationary points, the factor theorem, distance and midpoint, and the matrices for each transformation of the unit square.

sources.name: AQA Level 2 Certificate in Further Maths specification (8365)

resources.statusNote: None of these is on the formulae sheet. Several are results rather than formulae, such as the factor theorem, but questions expect you to use them without being told.

items.name: Differentiating a power
items.symbols: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is the gradient of the curve at any point. Multiply by the power, then take one off the power. It works for any integer $n$, and a constant differentiates to $0$. So $y = 4x^3 - 5x + 7$ gives $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 12x^2 - 5$. Expand brackets and split fractions first: $y = \dfrac{3}{x^2} = 3x^{-2}$ gives $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -6x^{-3}$.

items.name: Tangent and normal
items.symbols: The tangent touches the curve at the point and has the curve's gradient there. The normal goes through the same point at right angles to the tangent. Find $m$ from $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at the point, then use $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$. For $y = x^2 + 1$ at $(2, 5)$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2x = 4$, so the tangent is $y - 5 = 4(x - 2)$, which is $y = 4x - 3$. The normal has gradient $-\tfrac{1}{4}$: $y - 5 = -\tfrac{1}{4}(x - 2)$.

items.name: Stationary points
items.symbols: A stationary point is where the gradient is $0$: the top of a hill or the bottom of a dip. Differentiate again to get $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$: more than $0$ is a minimum, less than $0$ is a maximum. If it is $0$, check the sign of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ either side instead. For $y = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 - 6x - 9 = 3(x - 3)(x + 1)$, so $x = 3$ or $x = -1$. $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6x - 6$ is $12$ at $x = 3$, a minimum at $(3, -22)$, and $-12$ at $x = -1$, a maximum at $(-1, 10)$.

items.name: The factor theorem
items.formula: $f(a) = 0 \iff (x - a) \text{ is a factor of } f(x)$
items.symbols: The arrow means each side makes the other true. For $f(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x - 6$, $f(2) = 8 + 8 - 10 - 6 = 0$, so $(x - 2)$ is a factor. When the root is a fraction: $f\left(\tfrac{q}{p}\right) = 0 \iff (px - q)$ is a factor. For $f(x) = 2x^3 + x^2 - 8x - 4$, $f\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = 0$, so $(2x + 1)$ is a factor.

items.name: Distance between two points
items.symbols: Pythagoras on the change in $x$ and the change in $y$. From $(1, 2)$ to $(4, 6)$: $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$

items.name: Midpoint
items.symbols: The mean of the $x$ values and the mean of the $y$ values. For $(1, 2)$ and $(4, 6)$ it is $(2.5, 4)$

items.name: Perpendicular gradients
items.symbols: Lines at right angles. Gradients $2$ and $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ multiply to $-1$

items.name: The identity matrix
items.symbols: Leaves every point where it is: $IA = AI = A$

items.name: Enlargement, scale factor $k$, centre the origin
Rotation 270° anticlockwise (90° clockwise) about the origin

blocks.body:
**The unit square** has corners $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(1, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$.

**Using a matrix.** Write the point as a column and multiply: $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \times 2 + (-1) \times 3 \\ 1 \times 2 + 0 \times 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$, so $(2, 3)$ rotates to $(-3, 2)$.

**Checking a matrix.** The first column is where $(1, 0)$ goes and the second is where $(0, 1)$ goes. For a rotation of $90^\circ$ anticlockwise, $(1, 0)$ moves to $(0, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$ to $(-1, 0)$, which gives the columns $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$.

**Two in turn.** $A$ then $B$ is the single matrix $BA$: the first one goes on the right. Reflect in the $x$-axis, then rotate $90^\circ$ anticlockwise: $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, a reflection in $y = x$.

applications.title: Computer graphics
applications.body: Every time a game turns or mirrors a character, it multiplies each point by a matrix like these. Two moves in a row are one matrix multiplied by another.

applications.title: Getting the most from a sheet of card
applications.body: Cut a square of side $x$ cm from each corner of a 12 cm square of card and fold up the sides to make a box. Its volume is $V = x(12 - 2x)^2 = 4x^3 - 48x^2 + 144x$. Setting $\dfrac{dV}{dx} = 12x^2 - 96x + 144 = 0$ gives $x = 2$ or $x = 6$. At $x = 6$ there is no card left, so $x = 2$, and the box holds $128$ cm³, the most this card can.
